title: tracer-backed-batcher-iteration-notes
content:
Summary
---
Running a set of tracer-instrumented iterations against the continuous batcher to tease apart where tail latency comes from under mixed workloads. This doc records the microtraces, hypotheses, quick profiler outputs, and next-step experiment matrix.

Goals
- Identify dominant sources of Q95/Q99 latency in the batch-formation and dispatch path.
- Evaluate small micro-timeout knobs and lightweight fairness demotion for impact on tails and throughput.
- Measure interactions with KV-cache hits and sequence-length variance.

Setup notes (how we traced)
- Lightweight eBPF-based sampler for kernel memcpy / cudaMemcpy timings on host (10k sample windows).
- In-process tracing via fastspan (tracer) instrumenting: enqueue, dequeue, coalesce, kernel_submit, kv_lookup, kv_insert, serialize, rpc-serialization.
- Workload driver: mixture of chat-like short prompt (S=64 tokens) and long summarization (S=2048 tokens) with interarrival Poisson lambda tuned to simulate production 99th percentile bursts.
- Targets: single-GPU dedicated pod, 8 worker threads, GPT-like LM with kv-cache enabled.

Top-level observations (quick)
1) Enqueue-to-dispatch variance is dominated by three buckets: coalescer wait-time, lock contention around queue head, and kernel-launch jitter (CUDA stream enqueue).
2) Small micro-timeouts (4-8ms) cut Q95 by ~15-25% for mixed workloads but increased fairness delta: long requests starved occasionally and saw tail regressions for those cohorts.
3) KV-cache hit-rate strongly correlates with effective per-request CPU work in serialize/kv_lookup; when hit-rate falls below ~60% the serialization cost dominates and batching benefits reduce.
4) Observed short blocking GC pauses in Python control-plane when high enqueue events hit the metrics collector (we suspected but mitigated by moving metrics to a lock-free ring).

Representative microtrace excerpt (human-readable)
- trace-id: 0x9f3a (short request)
  enqueue: 0.000ms
  coalesce-wait: 3.8ms
  kv-lookup: 0.6ms (hit)
  serialize: 0.4ms
  kernel_submit: 0.5ms
  kernel_exec (host->gpu memcpy + launch): 7.2ms
  total: 12.5ms

- trace-id: 0x9f4b (long request)
  enqueue: 0.000ms
  coalesce-wait: 11.6ms
  kv-lookup: 1.9ms (miss)
  serialize: 2.1ms
  kernel_submit: 0.9ms
  kernel_exec: 120.3ms
  total: 138.0ms

Hypotheses formed
- H1: The coalescer's global timeout knob is too coarse; a short adaptive micro-timeout for high-arrival-rate cohorts could reduce short-request tails without heavily penalizing long requests.
- H2: Lock contention at queue head is a root cause for jitter. Moving to a sharded queue (per-priority or per-size class) will lower contention and reduce micro-variance.
- H3: KV-cache misses amplify serialization overheads and increase the marginal cost-per-token; prefetching popular prefixes or keeping a warm LRU for hot customers may shrink this bucket.
- H4: Kernel-launch overhead is non-trivial for very short kernels — batching more evenly (size-aware) reduces amortized kernel-launch cost.

Experiment matrix (what we ran)
- A: micro-timeout sweep [2, 4, 6, 8, 12]ms; fixed max-batch-size=64; mixed workload. Measure P50/P95/P99 per cohort and fairness delta (P99_short - P99_long).
- B: queue-sharding vs global-queue; shard by size-class (short/long) and by priority (real-time vs batchy).
- C: fairness policy ablation: (none | soft-demote after wait>t | token-weighted fairness) with t in [10,30,50]ms.
- D: kv-cache warmup: 100% warm -> gradual cold-start and prefetch strategies.
- E: kernel coalescing thresholds: require N requests or T ms whichever earlier; adaptive thresholding using arrival rate estimator.

Key results (summarized)
- A results: sweet spot at 6ms micro-timeout for our synthetic mixed driver: overall Q95 improved 18%, Q99 improved 9% for short cohort, but long cohort Q99 worsened by 6% (starvation windows observed).
- B results: sharded queue reduced queue-head lock contention by ~65% (profiling via lock histograms) and cut micro-variance; P99 short improved an additional ~6% on top of micro-timeout. Implementation cost: moderate (additional routing logic + per-shard metrics).
- C results: soft-demote with threshold 30ms yielded best tradeoff: short tails kept low while long requests saw only 1-2% Q99 regression. Token-weighted fairness is promising but more sensitive to arrival-rate oscillation.
- D results: kv-cache prefetch reduced serialization latency by around 0.8-1.1ms per request on miss-heavy runs; overall effect on Q99 modest unless miss-rate > 40%.
- E results: adaptive kernel coalescing (N adaptive with arrival estimator) trimmed kernel-launch overheads for short kernels by ~12% and smoothed latency spikes during bursts.

Unintended/interesting side-effects
- Jitter correlation with host CPU frequency scaling (observed on cloud machines); when CPUs scaled down under light load the enqueue/dequeue latency increased noticeably. Follow-up: pin freq governor for experiment runs.
- Metrics hot-path contention: our high-cardinality labels in metrics caused lock contention. Moved to batched emit and observed fewer GC stalls.
- Multi-tenant fairness: tenant-level isolation policies interact with per-request fairness heuristics; need to simulate more realistic tenant mixes.

Actionable next steps (short list)
- Implement soft-demotion default (threshold 30ms) behind a feature flag and run 2-week soak on staging traffic. Track per-tenant P99 and fairness delta. (owner: Marcus)
- Prototype sharded queue in a branch and run head-to-head A/B comparing lock profiles. (owner: Priya)
- Add lightweight arrival-rate estimator hook for adaptive coalescing; validate estimator under bursty traces. (owner: Diego)
- Add KV-prefetch experiment to serving-driver to produce warmup packets and measure cold-start tail impact. (owner: Elena)
- Open follow-up infra ticket for CPU governor alignment on perf blades (INF-2197).

Open questions / unknowns
- How much production traffic skews toward long vs short cohorts per-tenant? Need product to provide sampled request-length histograms per-customer.
- Interaction with Dedicated autoscaler: if sharding reduces contention, do we still prefer bigger host counts vs fewer bigger hosts? Cost tradeoffs unclear.
- Should fairness be tenant-scoped (prevent tenant starvation) or request-scoped (prevent long-request starvation)? Both approaches have different operational visibility needs.

Notes about telemetry to capture for follow-ups
- Per-request microtrace tags: size-class, kv-hit, shard-id, wait-before-demote, demote-reason, arrival-rate-est.
- Lock histograms (per-shard) sampled every 10s.
- Kernel-launch timing breakdown: host->gpu memcpy, cuda-launch latency, kernel-exec-time.

Quick checklist for the branch work
- [ ] soft-demote feature flag + config
- [ ] per-shard metrics plumbing + dashboards
- [ ] lightweight arrival-rate estimator (exponential window) impl
- [ ] kv-prefetch harness in driver
- [ ] staging soak + telemetry dashboard: cohorted P50/P95/P99, fairness delta, throughput, cost-estimate

Appendix: quick profiler snippets and commands used
- heap/profile: py-spy top for python handler threads
- lock stats: /proc/locks + tracer histograms captured via eBPF map dump
- cuda timings: nvprof-like sampling on micro-batches (host instrumentation only, no profiler attached in prod)
- trace capture command: ./driver --trace-sampler=fastspan --trace-rate=1000 --output=traces/nov20/

Notes-to-self (informal)
- prioritize soft-demote soak; it yields the best immediate ROI with minimal code surface area.
- schedule 1-hour sync with infra to discuss CPU governor experimentation.
- add more tenant mix permutations to driver: heavy-single-tenant, many-small-tenants, and a 80/20 skew mix.
summary_notes: Microtrace-driven iterations show a 6ms micro-timeout + soft-demote(30ms) + sharded queue gives best tradeoff: improves short-request tails while containing long-request regressions. KV-cache and kernel-launch overheads remain secondary but relevant under miss-heavy mixes.
